Make the TemplatedDictionary objects picklable

The jinja2 SandboxedEnvironment objects are not guaranteed to be
pickle-serializable (even though they practically are).  So let's rather
store the environment elsewhere than in the TemplatedDictionary object
itself to keep it serializable.

Nb. TemplatedDictionary is just a wrapper around dict, which is quite
commonly subject of (de)serialization (e.g. Mock, the main user of
templated-dictionary library does that through the
concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor logic).

It would be disadvantageous to introduce additional internal arguments
into the object itself (considering we already have the __jinja_expand
internal).

Having a per-application shared environment is kind of expected anyway
(and even more optimal):

    https://jinja.palletsprojects.com/en/3.0.x/api/#basics

Note that this fix is mostly needed for the RHEL 8 environment with
jinja2 v2.10.1; newer versions made the environments (namely the
included filters) picklable: https://github.com/pallets/jinja/pull/1613

explanation:
security: nOAuth defense, verification-token purpose binding, admin sessions (#748)

Pre-release audit remediation for 2.4.0: findings F1-F5, F11, F14. (Prefixed
F- rather than written bare: a `#1` renders as a link to an unrelated issue.)

F1/F2 nOAuth account takeover via social login
  Federated logins resolved a local account from a provider-asserted email
  with no attestation behind it. Entra v2 tokens carry no email_verified at
  all and `email` is a mutable directory attribute, so a free attacker-owned
  tenant could assert a victim's address and land in their session.

  Every provider now reports its own real signal, Microsoft tokens are pinned
  to a trusted tenant (or xms_edov), and an unattested address may not select
  a local account. --oauth-allow-unverified-provider-email is a narrowed
  compatibility ramp: it still cannot cross into an account another credential
  owns.

F3 verification-token purpose confusion
  Magic-link, signup, invite and forgot-password tokens shared one table keyed
  by token alone, and no consumer checked purpose. A leaked magic link was
  redeemable at ResetPassword for durable account takeover.

  Gated at all three consumers, not just the GraphQL pair: GET /verify_email
  is a separate implementation of the same flow and is the URL the mails
  actually point at, so gating only the mutations would have left a
  forgot-password token redeemable there for a full session.

F4/F14 admin session and secret
  The admin cookie was bcrypt(AdminSecret): no expiry, no revocation, logout
  could not invalidate a captured copy. Now an opaque server-side handle.

  Both admin-secret comparison paths share one throttled gate. It counts
  FAILED attempts only — it runs on every x-authorizer-admin-secret request,
  so counting successes would 401 a concurrent admin API client presenting the
  correct secret. MetaFromGRPC now falls back to the gRPC peer address, so the
  counter is keyed per caller instead of collapsing to one bucket shared by
  every gRPC client (where a handful of wrong guesses locked out all of them).

F5 per-account login lockout, F11 single-use TOTP passcodes (RFC 6238 5.2).

Also bounds the pre-hijack delete to accounts holding no state. The cascade
(#749) destroys those rows rather than orphaning them, but an unauthenticated
callback still must not take out an account's org memberships, MFA enrollment
or FGA grants to resolve an email collision, and FGA tuples are outside the
cascade entirely. Makes resend_verify_email able to mint a fresh request, and
makes email verification with no SMTP a fatal misconfiguration.

change and verified closed after.

  email matched an arbitrary user without knowing any address. Added string
  type guards, which also cover the array form that mongoose's own
  sanitizeFilter does not catch.

- /view-{cardio,dia,lung}-report returned any user's clinical record by id
  along with the owner's real name. The handlers already resolved the owner
  and never compared it to the caller. Ownership is derived from the User
  array rather than a userId column because LungData has no such field.

- /api/job-status and /api/job-result had no auth at all, and BullMQ assigns
  sequential integer ids, so results were enumerable. Jobs now carry the
  submitting userId and both routes verify it. Raw Python stderr is no longer
  returned to the client.

- /api/signup accepted an attacker-supplied groupId, and switch-profile then
  minted a token for any member of that group without a password. groupId is
  no longer read from the body.

  GET /. password is now select:false and every response is projected.

* feat: Agents — send one conversation to an assistant that is not on this machine

Turing's own assistant stays the default and the only local one. Agents adds
the ability to configure Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok or any OpenAI-compatible
endpoint, and to hand a chosen conversation to one of them.

Routing is per conversation and only ever by hand. Nothing is inferred and
nothing is global: a conversation goes where someone sent it, and every other
conversation stays here. The destination is read inside the same transaction
that accepts the message and frozen into the job payload, so re-pointing or
deleting an agent cannot redirect a message already sent — it must not be
possible for a transcript to arrive at a company the user did not pick.

Because this is the one feature that breaks the local-first promise on purpose,
it says so where the user is looking rather than in a settings screen:

  - A strip above the conversation names the destination at all times, and
    turns amber with "messages leave your machine" when that destination is off
    it. A failed read says it does not know, never "stays on your machine" —
    reassurance after a failed read is the one lie that strip exists to prevent.
  - Each routed message writes a notice into the transcript itself, naming the
    agent, the endpoint host and the model, in the same transaction that queues
    the run.
  - Cross-session recall is disabled for routed runs. The user opted ONE
    conversation into leaving; recall draws on conversations they never chose to
    send anywhere, and widening consent silently is exactly the surprise the
    first commitment forbids. Capability loses to consent, and the picker says
    so.

Credentials: the database stores a credential NAME, never a key. There is no
column that could hold one, and a test asserts that. The keys live in
TURING_AGENT_API_KEYS in turing-backend/.env — one JSON object of
name -> key — so adding an agent from the client never needs a compose edit.
The agent runtime is the only process that reads the values; the orchestrator
parses the same variable but keeps only the names, which is enough to tell the
client an agent will not work yet instead of letting them find out by sending a
message. No key is ever written to SQLite, put on a job payload, sent over the
runtime stream, or handed to a client.

All four vendors expose an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint, so this
is the existing openai_compatible provider configured per job — one client, not
four integrations. A plaintext http endpoint is refused unless it is on this
machine, since the whole conversation travels over that URL.

Left unwired, a routed job fails with external_agent_unavailable rather than
being answered locally under another assistant's name; a missing key fails with
a message naming the credential and the file it belongs in.

that back found three defects in a row, each masking the next.

1. Credentials were looked up under one name only.

A PingOne Worker app IS the Management API client, and this environment has one

from one prefix and the secret from another gives a mismatched pair that fails
as invalid_client, which reads as a bad secret rather than a bad pairing.
(configStore's chains at ~1106-1107 resolve the two independently and carry the
same latent hazard — noted in a comment, not changed here.)

PINGONE_ADMIN_* is excluded even though configStore's chain includes it. In this
environment that is "Demo AI App - Admin Login", a WEB_APP whose grants are

in an application/x-www-form-urlencoded body. PingOne mis-parsed the request and
answered with errors about the AUTH METHOD and the GRANT TYPE, neither of which
was wrong. Now built with URLSearchParams.

A self-contained ALARM channel that raises a phone when a real alarm condition
fires in amplifier-work-tracker. Lives in
`src/amplifier_work_tracker/webpush.py`. It adopts the wire shape proven by
Amplifier's notify bundle (`hooks-notify-push`) and adds the three things an
*alarm* channel needs and that bundle lacks: **Bearer auth** for a self-hosted
ntfy, **`Priority: urgent`** (bypasses phone Do-Not-Disturb), and a **bounded
retry + LOUD fail** (never a silent swallow).

## Wire shape

```
POST {NTFY_SERVER}/{NTFY_TOPIC}
Title: <title>
Priority: urgent
Tags: rotating_light,warning
Click: <optional dashboard deep-link>
Authorization: Bearer <NTFY_TOKEN>     # only when a token is configured

<message as raw UTF-8 body bytes>
```

## Configuration (env only — secrets never in a settings file)

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NTFY_SERVER` | `https://ntfy.sh` | ntfy base URL. Point at your self-hosted instance. |
| `NTFY_TOPIC` | *(unset)* | Topic. On public ntfy.sh the topic name **is** the password — keep it in the env, never a file. |
| `NTFY_TOKEN` | *(unset)* | Self-hosted access token, sent as `Authorization: Bearer`. Optional. |
| `NTFY_ALARM_ENABLED` | *(unset)* | Enable flag (`1`/`true`/`yes`/`on`). Opt-in: while unset, `send_alarm` is a safe no-op. |
| `NTFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` | `4` | Retry budget (attempts, not retries). |
| `NTFY_BACKOFF_BASE_SECONDS` | `0.5` | Base for exponential backoff between attempts. |
| `NTFY_CLICK_BASE` | *(unset)* | Optional dashboard base URL for a `Click:` deep-link back to the item. |

### Why self-hosted + token (recommended for this deployment)

This deployment runs behind Tailscale. A private self-hosted ntfy plus an
access token removes the "topic name == password" fragility of public ntfy.sh:
the topic can no longer be guessed off the wire, and delivery is authenticated.

## Retry + LOUD fail semantics

- **2xx** → delivered.
- **Transient** (network/timeout error, HTTP `429`, or any `5xx`) → retried up
  to `NTFY_MAX_ATTEMPTS` with exponential backoff.
- **Exhausted retries, or a non-transient `4xx`** → `logger.error(...)` **and**
  `AlarmDeliveryError`. The `logger.error` is deliberately NOT debug-only (the
  way `hooks-notify-push` logs) — it is the line that must appear in the journal
  when the phone did not ring.
- **Disabled** (`NTFY_ALARM_ENABLED` not truthy) → no-op result, so call sites
  can invoke it unconditionally.

## The trigger — bound to the already-trusted signal

The alarm keys off the **custody-TTL breach**, i.e. the exact signal the reaper
already trusts: `custody.reclaim_eligible(record) -> (eligible, reason)`. It
does **not** re-decide eligibility and is **not** wired to any new/unproven
ranking logic. Helpers in `webpush.py`:

- `reclaim_alarm_payload(item_id, holder, reason)` — pure `(title, message, tags, click)` formatting.
- `alarm_for_reclaimed_item(item_id, holder, reason, ...)` — async, formats + sends (urgent).
- `fire_reclaim_alarm(item_id, holder, reason, config=None)` — **sync, never-raises** entry point for the reap-sweep worker thread.

## 1. Trust Model in One Sentence

> Any holder of the primary API token can do anything the owner of the server can do via Chroxy — read every session's history, send input to any session, switch models, change permission modes, and modify settings. Pairing-bound session tokens are scoped to one session. Per-session hook secrets are scoped to one session **and** to the CLI permission-hook callback endpoint (`POST /permission`) only — they are never accepted for user-facing permission-response handling. The daemon-level ingest secret is scoped to the ingest/mailbox endpoints (`POST /api/events`, `POST /api/mailbox*`): it feeds the notification pipeline and can trigger a bounded, fixed-string mailbox wakeup into an idle claude-tui recipient — but grants no reads (see §6).

The server is the user's own machine (see [`encryption-threat-model.md` §2](encryption-threat-model.md#2-trust-boundaries)). The primary token is therefore deliberately equivalent to local access on that machine.
